WIC, explained · 8–10 minutes

Why do families
miss out on WIC?

Women. Infants. Children.

That’s what WIC stands for. Its full name is the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children.

Getting enrolled is only the beginning. Families still have to understand what they can buy, use their benefits, and keep them active.

Start with what WIC does ↓
WICFood benefits

Written by Megan Quigley

First, what is WIC for?

Help families get the nutrition they need early in life.

Pregnancy, infancy, and early childhood are important periods for growth and health. WIC is a federal program for eligible low-income pregnant and postpartum women, infants, and children under five who have a nutrition-related need.

It provides specific foods, nutrition advice, breastfeeding support, and referrals to health care. It supplements a family’s food budget; it isn’t meant to pay for every grocery.

A benefit card is not the finish line. The question is whether families can understand and use the support they have been given. Start with what it can pay for.

See the grocery example ↓

01 / An example grocery trip

An eligible child’s groceries
could cost the family less.

This example uses a California food package for an eligible four-year-old. The groceries stay the same; the payment changes.

They pick up milk. Crossing it off means it’s in the cart.

They add eggs and whole-wheat bread.

Then peanut butter, apples, frozen peas, and dish soap.

The family buys all seven items. Next, we’ll see which ones WIC could pay for—and how much that changes the bill.

02 / What’s covered

Food quantities plus
money for fruit and vegetables.

WIC’s food package has two parts: set amounts of approved foods, plus a separate fruit-and-vegetable dollar balance. The $26 is not the value of the whole package.

Blue means WIC can cover a qualifying product when that food is in the issued package and enough balance remains.

WIC won’t pay for dish soap. With the approved foods and enough benefits, though, it can cover the rest of this basket. Here’s the price difference.

03 / At the checkout

WIC could cover $19.14
of this $22.63 grocery bill.

Both baskets contain the same groceries. Being eligible does not pay for them by itself.

On the right, approved foods move to the WIC side of the bill. The household still pays for the soap.

WIC would cover $19.14 of this $22.63 basket. But qualifying isn’t enough: the family must be enrolled and have benefits available. How many eligible people do?

What if a child received this support from age one until their fifth birthday? Buying this basket once a month would shift $918.72 from the household to WIC over four years, at these fixed prices. This is an illustration, not a forecast.

04 / Participation nationwide

Being eligible doesn’t mean
receiving WIC.

Qualifying for WIC and receiving it are different. Here’s how many eligible people actually participate.

An estimated 11.8 million people were eligible in an average month in 2023. About 6.6 million participated.

That national rate includes infants, children, and pregnant or postpartum women. When we separate children by age, a much bigger gap appears.

Source and details ↗

USDA combines modeled eligibility estimates with administrative participant counts. Gap = 11,829,215 eligible − 6,631,309 participants = 5,197,906. The grid rounds 56.1% to 56 marks. Includes eligible infants, children, and pregnant/postpartum women; not just children. Tables 3.1 and 3.5.

05 / Before kindergarten

By age four, only 26.9%
of eligible children receive WIC.

Among eligible infants, WIC reaches 82.3%.

At age one, that share is 67.4%. At two, 52.5%.

By age three, 45.2%. By four, just 26.9%.

Children ages one through four make up 76% of the total gap. They can still qualify. To understand why so many aren’t receiving WIC, let’s look at where families live and how they get help.

06 / Participation by state

Where a family lives
changes the participation picture.

Each dot is a state. Its color shows the share of eligible people receiving WIC.

The national average is 56.1%. But that average hides substantial differences.

California: 72.4%. Louisiana: 41.3%. That is a 31.1-percentage-point gap.

The same dots now line up by coverage. The thin lines show uncertainty around each estimate.

Vermont’s estimate is 79.6%, with a wide uncertainty interval. These estimates show differences—not what caused them.

All eligible groups · average month in 2023 · DC and Puerto Rico shown separately.

Source and details ↗

USDA Table 3.5. Average monthly eligibility and participation, CY2023; all categories combined. Intervals are reported 95% Wald confidence intervals. The map includes 50 states, DC, and Puerto Rico. Other territories are included in national estimates but not individually reported. Population differences, estimation uncertainty, and program conditions all matter.

07 / Already connected

Other programs reach children
that WIC still misses.

Some of the children missing from WIC already participate in two other assistance programs.

Another program can establish income eligibility. It does not automatically enroll a child in WIC.

Better referrals may help. But an introduction to WIC is only the beginning. Families still have to complete the steps to get and use it.

08 / Steps to get and use WIC

Enrolled doesn’t mean
ready to use the benefit.

A card does not explain every rule. Families need to understand their food quantities, produce dollars, and benefit-use dates.

Then there’s the work of enrolling and renewing: information to gather, appointments to attend, and time to find around work or caregiving. The benefit has a time cost.

Finally, shopping has its own rules. Two similar egg cartons can have different approval status. Enrollment doesn’t remove the work of using the benefit. That helps explain why benefit use deserves a closer look.

What a family has to manage

  1. Understand the rulesUnderstand the balance, approved foods, and benefit-use dates.
  2. Make time to enroll and renewGather information. Complete appointments and follow-up requirements.
  3. Use the benefits in a storeCheck the balance. Find the approved food, size, and variety.

A balance is more than a dollar amount.

Food quantities plus produce dollars. Approved types and sizes. A date to use them by.

Clear instructions matter after enrollment, too.

09 / Using food benefits

Even enrolled families
don’t always use all their benefits.

Receiving food benefits doesn’t mean using all of them. A Southern California study measured how much participants used.

Each percentage shows how often participants used at least 70% of that food benefit during a certification period. These are local study results.

Using very little was linked to leaving WIC afterward, though it wasn’t proven to cause it. That raises another question: does staying in WIC matter for children’s diets?

Longitudinal study of 188,368 Southern California WIC participants; Nov. 2019–June 2023. Food-category percentages use certification periods with that category issued as the denominator. Discontinuation: no benefits issued for two months after the certification period. Overall redemption comparison: under 10% versus ≥70%. Observational; participants differ, and continuing eligibility is not established by this comparison.

10 / Beyond enrollment

Staying in WIC longer was linked
to better diets at age three.

The study compared children who received WIC only in their first year with children who continued into their third year.

At age three, the longer-participation group scored 3.6 points higher on diet quality. Higher means better.

This is a reason to care about continued access. It is an association, not proof that WIC caused the difference.

No absolute scores or invented food servings are shown. Residual differences between groups may help explain the association.

11 / Changes that may help

Changing how benefits work
can help more children participate.

Child coverage rose from 43.5% in 2016 to 47.9% in 2023. The difference from infant coverage persists.

A separate national study examined the shift from paper benefits to electronic cards. Child participation increased following implementation.

Electronic cards don’t explain the whole national trend. But this study suggests that making benefits easier to use can help more children receive support.

These are different analyses and outcomes; no causal link between this intervention and the entire plotted trend is implied.

12 / Keeping support accessible

Food support only helps
if families can keep using it.

WIC’s food support can make a real difference to a grocery bill. For more families to receive it, the program needs to be easy to enroll in, shop with, and keep using.

Sources and next steps

Resources

WIC can support children until they turn five, but many eligible children don’t receive it. The research suggests several areas to examine: whether families know they still qualify, how other programs refer them, how easy benefits are to use, and what helps families stay enrolled. There isn’t one proven explanation.

Need WIC information?

WIC serves eligible pregnant and postpartum people, infants, and children under five. Your local agency can check the requirements and explain your food package.
